### Study Population

The Age, Gene/Environment Susceptibility-Reykjavik Study (AGES-Reykjavik) is a population-based cohort study initiated in 2002 as a continuation of the Reykjavik Study, which had followed residents of Reykjavik, Iceland since 1967 [@RN1]. The AGES-Reykjavik cohort was drawn from surviving members of the original Reykjavik Study cohort (born 1907-1935). Study protocols were approved by the National Bioethics Committee in Iceland (VSN-00-063), the National Institute on Aging Intramural Institutional Review Board, and the Icelandic Data Protection Authority. All participants provided written informed consent.

The present analysis included 2,491 participants with available DNA methylation data and dementia diagnoses [(@tbl-dementia-category)]{.rev}, comprising 1,065 males (42.8%) and 1,426 females (57.2%). [At baseline, the mean (standard deviation) age was 75.9 (5.2) years.]{.rev} Smoking status was classified as non-smoker (n=1,088, 43.7%), former smoker (n=1,118, 44.9%), or current smoker (n=285, 11.4%). [Baseline characteristics by group are given in @tbl-baseline.]{.rev}

### Dementia Assessment and Classification

[Cognitive status was classified at the baseline examination (AGES-I, 2002–2006), at which the blood sample for DNA methylation was drawn, and again at the follow-up examination (AGES-II, 2007–2011), a median of 5.1 years later (@suppfig-timeline).]{.rev} Dementia diagnoses followed a three-step process including initial cognitive screening of the total baseline sample, detailed neuropsychological testing for step 1 screen-positives, and among those who screened positive in step 2, a comprehensive neurologic examination and a proxy interview. Final diagnoses, based on the totality of data collected by questionnaire, depression, physical and sensory function, and laboratory data were adjudicated by a consensus panel (geriatrician, neurologist, neuroradiologist, and neuropsychologist) and diagnosed following international criteria. [Because MCI is not typically recorded in the health records used for follow-up, and to keep its diagnosis standardized, MCI was assessed only at the AGES-I and AGES-II examinations. Incident dementia (601 participants) was diagnosed at AGES-II or identified through record linkage to nursing-home assessments, home-care assessments and death certificates up to 4 October 2015 [@RN1; @RN63]. The 2,330 participants without dementia at baseline were followed to dementia diagnosis, death or the end of surveillance for a mean of 9.7 years (maximum 13.4 years); the follow-up times in @tbl-dementia-category are defined by group, as stated in its footnotes.]{.rev}
 
Based on cognitive status at baseline and follow-up, participants were categorized into six groups (@tbl-dementia-category). Of the 2,174 participants who were cognitively normal at baseline, 1,581 (72.7%) maintained normal cognition throughout follow-up (stable normal), 99 (4.6%) progressed to mild cognitive impairment (normal2mci), and 494 (22.7%) developed incident dementia (normal2incid). Among 156 participants diagnosed with MCI at baseline, 49 (31.4%) remained cognitively stable (stable_mci), and 107 (68.6%) progressed to dementia (mci2incid). [MCI was re-assessed only at the follow-up examination, at which all 99 normal2mci, 1,478 of the 1,581 stable normal and 26 of the 49 stable_mci participants were classified; the other 103 stable normal and 23 stable_mci participants were classified from records by the absence of a recorded dementia diagnosis (@suppfig-timeline), so unobserved MCI or reversion, respectively, cannot be ruled out for them.]{.rev} The remaining 161 participants (6.5%) had prevalent dementia at study entry. Notably, no participants in the normal2mci or stable_mci groups progressed to dementia during the 13.4-year follow-up period.

### Processing of DNA Methylation Data

::: {.rev}
Whole blood-derived DNA samples from the baseline (AGES-I) examination, together with samples from the AGES-II examination, were bisulfite-converted and assayed at the Huge-F facility at Erasmus Medical Center (Rotterdam, the Netherlands) on the Illumina Infinium MethylationEPIC BeadChip v1, manifest B5 (Illumina Inc., San Diego, CA, USA), which carries 865,918 probes. The 4,696 samples were arrayed on 49 plates of 96 wells and 587 BeadChips of eight samples each. The BeadChips were scanned on Illumina iScan systems (iScan Control Software 4.0) between 30 September and 24 December 2021. Only AGES-I samples were analyzed in the present study.
:::

::: {.rev}
Quality control was performed by the facility in R (v4.0.5) with the minfi, meffil and ewastools packages [@RN64; @RN65; @RN66]. At the sample level, 20 control metrics from the Illumina BeadArray Controls Reporter were compared with Illumina's recommended cut-offs. Of the 18 samples flagged, 9 met the criteria for failure (poor bisulfite conversion or bisulfite-conversion background, hybridization, specificity or extension) and were excluded, including all 5 samples with a call rate of 0.96 or less (detection *P* > 0.01 at 4% or more of probes); the other 9 were judged sub-optimal and retained, leaving 4,687 samples. At the probe level, 46,116 probes were removed (the categories overlap): 1,851 with detection *P* > 0.01 in more than 10% of samples, 1,258 with a bead count < 3 in more than 10% of samples, 43,254 cross-reactive probes, and 998 probes flagged by Illumina as problematic on manifest B5, leaving 819,802 probes.

The facility normalized all 4,687 samples together by quantile normalization within six probe categories (QN-6C), the normalization step of the CPACOR pipeline [@RN104]. We kept the autosomal CpG probes, removing 2,595 non-CpG ('ch') probes and 18,058 probes on the X and Y chromosomes, which left 799,149 CpG sites. Normalized β-values were converted to M-values, M = log~2~[β/(1 − β)], which were used for all statistical analyses because of their better statistical properties for differential methylation analysis [@RN99].

Of the 2,602 participants with an AGES-I sample that passed quality control, we excluded 46 whose MCI at baseline had reverted to normal cognition at follow-up and 60 whose cognitive status at the end of follow-up was unknown, leaving 2,496 participants in the six groups; a further 5 with missing smoking status were excluded, leaving 2,491 for analysis.
:::


### Dementia Association Analysis

We performed an epigenome-wide association study (EWAS) testing differential DNA methylation across dementia trajectory groups. For each of the 799,149 CpG sites, methylation M-values were regressed on dementia status, adjusting for age, sex, smoking status, and six white blood cell type proportions: M-value~i~ = β~0~ + β~1~·dementia_status + β~2~·age + β~3~·sex + β~4~·smoking + β~5–10~·WBC_proportions + ε~i~. [To check for batch effects, we added array plate number (1–49) to the model as an additional numeric covariate in a sensitivity analysis: the group effect estimates across all CpG sites correlated closely with the primary estimates (Pearson *r* 0.96–1.00 across the five contrasts), likely because the M-values had been quantile-normalized across all samples together. The estimates were also concordant with Alzheimer's disease effects in three external cohorts (see Comparison with published blood EWAS).]{.rev}

Dementia status was coded as a six-level categorical variable with stable normal cognition as the reference group, yielding five contrasts (stable_mci, normal2mci, normal2incid, mci2incid, and prevalent dementia). [The coefficient for each contrast (the elements of β~1~ in the model above) is the covariate-adjusted difference in mean M-value between that group and the stable normal group; this is the effect size (ΔM) reported throughout, and a positive ΔM indicates higher methylation than in the stable normal group.]{.rev} Sex was coded with male as the reference category and smoking status with non-smoker as the reference category. White blood cell proportions (B lymphocytes, CD4+ T lymphocytes, CD8+ T lymphocytes, monocytes, neutrophils, and eosinophils) were estimated from DNA methylation data using a reference-based deconvolution against purified leukocyte profiles [@RN67; @RN98] [(@tbl-baseline)]{.rev}.

Genome-wide significance was defined at *P* < 1.0 × 10^−8^, which is slightly more stringent than the Bonferroni correction for the number of CpG sites tested (0.05 / 799,149 = 6.26 × 10^−8^) and is consistent with empirically derived thresholds for epigenome-wide studies on the EPIC array [@RN74; @RN75]. Results are also presented at less stringent thresholds for sensitivity analyses. Analyses were conducted in R (v4.5.2) using `stats::lm()` for linear regression, with parallel processing via the furrr and future packages. Model results were extracted with `broom::tidy()`.

Ordinary linear regression was used rather than Cox proportional hazards models. The dementia trajectory classification involves multiple starting states (cognitively normal, MCI, prevalent dementia) and multiple endpoints, a multi-state structure that does not conform to the single-origin, time-to-event framework of survival models. Linear regression also provided a unified covariate-adjustment framework across the EWAS, the methylation-residual computation that feeds UMAP and VAE, and the downstream analyses. [Follow-up time was not entered as a covariate, because it is part of the group definitions: it ends at the diagnosis that defines the incident dementia groups, is zero for prevalent dementia and, in the stable groups, depends on survival. For the normal2mci group, classified at AGES-II, it varied little (mean 5.3 years, SD 0.4; @suppfig-timeline), and age at baseline was a covariate in the association model. We refitted the 403 DMPs after excluding the 62 participants without dementia who were followed for less than 5 years, all of whom had died: effect sizes were retained for the four contrasts whose own groups were unchanged (slope of refitted on original estimates at each contrast's own DMPs, 1.00–1.06; 322 of the 326 prevalent-dementia DMPs remained at *P* < 1.0 × 10^−8^) and attenuated for stable_mci (slope 0.72), which lost 10 of its 49 participants. To assess whether baseline cognition accounted for the associations, we refitted the model for the 403 DMPs with the three baseline cognitive composite scores (memory, processing speed and working memory; @tbl-baseline) added as covariates, in the 2,302 participants with all three scores, and compared the estimates with those of the same model without the composites in the same participants.]{.rev}

### Gene Annotation

We performed comprehensive gene annotation for CpG sites using both the Illumina (UCSC) gene annotation [@RN71] and the Genomic Regions Enrichment of Annotations Tool (GREAT) [@RN68]. For the GREAT analysis, we created a BED file containing genomic coordinates of all CpG sites from the Illumina MethylationEPIC BeadChip. Using the default "basal plus extension" approach, GREAT assigns each gene a regulatory domain that extends 5 kb upstream and 1 kb downstream from its transcription start site. This domain is then extended up to 1 Mb in both directions until reaching the regulatory domains of neighboring genes. Each CpG site is subsequently associated with all genes whose regulatory domains it overlaps, enabling a systematic mapping of potential regulatory relationships.


### Gene Ontology Enrichment Analysis

We performed Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis for biological processes using the enrichGO function from the clusterProfiler R package (version 4.16.0) [@RN69]. For each dementia transition, CpG sites were ranked by their association [*P* values]{.rev} from the genome-wide analysis, and the top 1,000 and 2,000 CpG sites were selected. Their corresponding GREAT-annotated genes were mapped to Entrez gene identifiers using the org.Hs.eg.db annotation database and used as input for enrichment analysis. This rank-based selection was adopted because applying a common genome-wide significance threshold produced highly unequal numbers of CpG sites across transitions, leaving some transition groups with too few genes for meaningful enrichment analysis. By selecting a fixed number of top-ranked CpG sites, comparable gene set sizes were obtained for each transition, enabling balanced comparison of enriched biological processes. The background gene set comprised all GREAT-annotated genes associated with CpG sites on the Illumina MethylationEPIC BeadChip. Enrichment was performed separately for each dementia transition and CpG threshold, using Gene Ontology biological process terms with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing. Enrichment was considered statistically significant at an adjusted [*P*]{.rev} < 0.05.

[To identify biological processes significant in only one group, we determined transition-specific GO terms, defined as terms significantly enriched in exactly one of the five groups.]{.rev} Commonly used redundancy reduction tools such as REVIGO and the simplify function in clusterProfiler compute pairwise semantic similarity among enriched terms and retain only the most significant representative from each cluster, effectively discarding the remaining terms. [Because this study aimed to comprehensively characterize the biological processes engaged at each disease stage rather than to produce a minimal list of non-redundant terms, we did not use these tools and instead counted the terms in a redundancy-aware way, in two steps. First, before determining the transition-specific terms, we removed exact duplicates: a significant parent term whose genes in the background set were identical to those of a significant child term, and which therefore had the same result in every group (5 terms among the top 1,000 CpG sites and 18 among the top 2,000). Second, because GO terms are nested and related terms can be enriched together, we weighted each transition-specific term by its immediate relatives in the GO graph, that is, its parent and child terms (GO.db version 3.21.0, GO release of 6 February 2025; is_a, part_of and regulates relations). A term none of whose immediate relatives was significant in any group counted as one term; otherwise, its weight was reduced by the share of its immediate relatives that were significant, in the same group or in another: *w* = 1 − *s*/*r*, where *r* is the number of the term's immediate relatives and *s* the number of these that were significant in at least one group. The numbers of transition-specific terms per group and per functional category are the sums of these weights, rounded to whole numbers; Data S7 and S8 give each term's weight.]{.rev}

Transition-specific GO terms were then grouped into functional categories to facilitate biological interpretation. [We defined 22 categories, our own grouping rather than part of GO, from the names and descriptions of the transition-specific GO terms, and a large language model assisted in selecting the keywords for each category. Each term was assigned to one category by matching its GO term name, ignoring case, against these keywords. Because a name can match more than one category, the categories were tested in a fixed order from specific to broad, not by clinical stage, and each term received the first category that matched: Synaptic Vesicle Control, Regulatory Mechanisms (miRNA transcription), Behavioral Response, Tissue Response, Cellular Homeostasis, Hypoxia Response, Extracellular Matrix Organization, Synaptic Function and Organization, Glial Cell Regulation, Ion Transport and Regulation, Immune Response, Neural Development and Regulation, Vascular Development, Hormone Signaling, Gene Regulation, Cell Cycle Regulation, Cell Migration and Organization, Cellular Metabolism, Cellular Transport, Cellular Signaling, Cellular Organization, and Development and Differentiation (e.g., "develop" or "differentiat"). Three categories carried exclusion rules: Tissue Response excluded terms containing "vascular", Ion Transport and Regulation excluded "exocytosis" and "metal ion", and Vascular Development excluded "cell migration". Of the 204 transition-specific terms from the top 1,000 CpG sites, 149 matched one category, 53 matched more than one and received the first in this order (for 45 of them, the other match was Development and Differentiation), and 2 matched none and remained unassigned; for the top 2,000 CpG sites, the corresponding numbers were 312, 106 and 13 of 431 terms. The order therefore affected only the terms that matched more than one category. The complete keyword rules are part of the analysis code (see Code availability).]{.rev} For example, terms related to extracellular matrix organization (GO:0030198), extracellular structure organization (GO:0043062), and positive regulation of collagen biosynthetic process (GO:0032967) were categorized under "Extracellular Matrix Organization". Similarly, terms involving regulation of postsynapse organization (GO:0099175), modulation of excitatory postsynaptic potential (GO:0098815), and postsynapse assembly (GO:0099068) were grouped under "Synaptic Function and Organization".

### UMAP Dimensionality Reduction

::: {.rev}
We applied Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) [@RN78] and a variational autoencoder (VAE; see below) to the same input at two significance thresholds: the 403 CpG sites with *P* < 1.0 × 10^−8^ and the 949 with *P* < 1.0 × 10^−7^ in at least one of the five contrasts with stable normal cognition. For each site, M-values were regressed on the EWAS covariates (age, sex, smoking status and the six white blood cell proportions) without dementia status, and the residuals were centered and scaled to unit variance across the 2,491 participants. UMAP was implemented with the uwot package (version 0.2.4) with n_neighbors = 10, min_dist = 0.5, n_components = 6 and the Euclidean distance metric.

The EWAS screen did not impose a linear trend across groups. Dementia status entered the EWAS as a categorical variable, so a site was selected if any one group differed from stable normal cognition, and each per-site model describes that site alone; UMAP and the VAE model how the selected sites vary together across participants, which may be nonlinear. A screen was needed because, with 799,149 sites and 2,491 participants, an embedding of the whole array would be expected to reflect mostly variation unrelated to dementia. Selecting CpG sites on their relation to the outcome before fitting an autoencoder to blood methylation data has precedent [@RN97]. The screen keeps only sites whose mean differs between groups, so sites related to dementia status only through joint patterns would be missed. Because the sites were selected for their association with dementia status, and the embedding settings below were chosen by inspecting (VAE) or scoring (UMAP) group separation, the embeddings describe the structure of the selected associations rather than testing them anew.
:::

To reduce sensitivity to random initialization, UMAP was run five times with different random seeds (123, 223, 323, 423, 523) and the resulting embeddings were averaged element-wise to produce a single stable representation per [participant]{.rev}. [The UMAP settings n_neighbors = 10 and min_dist = 0.5 were chosen in a pilot grid of 25 combinations of five n_neighbors values (10, 15, 20, 30, 50) and five min_dist values (0.01, 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8), scored with the dementia progression score (DPS; below). The combination n_neighbors = 10, min_dist = 0.5 gave the highest median DPS over the 15 dimension pairs at both thresholds, and the median DPS was positive for all 25 combinations.]{.rev}

### VAE Dimensionality Reduction

We also employed a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [@RN77], a deep learning method based on neural networks, to learn a probabilistic latent representation of DNA methylation patterns. While UMAP preserves local neighborhood structure through graph-based optimization, the VAE learns a generative model that captures nonlinear relationships through encoder-decoder neural networks, providing a complementary perspective on the underlying data structure.

The VAE architecture consisted of a symmetric encoder-decoder with four hidden layers (512, 256, 128, and 64 units) using ReLU activations, batch normalization, and dropout regularization (0.05–0.1). The encoder mapped input methylation values to a 6-dimensional latent space via the reparameterization trick, and the decoder reconstructed the original input from the latent representation. The model was trained using the Adam optimizer (learning rate = 0.001) with a composite loss function combining mean squared error for reconstruction and KL divergence for regularization, weighted by a beta parameter. [Reconstruction error was averaged over CpG sites and the KL term was summed over the six latent dimensions. Models were trained in batches of 256 for up to 150 epochs, with early stopping (patience 40 epochs; the weights with the lowest validation loss were kept) and learning-rate reduction on plateau (factor 0.5, patience 20 epochs, minimum 10⁻⁵); both callbacks monitored the loss on the held-out fold (see below). The architecture was chosen after exploratory pilot runs that included shallower autoencoder and VAE variants.]{.rev}

[The β weight on the Kullback–Leibler term was set to 0.001 after a pilot sweep of eight values (0.0001, 0.0003, 0.0006, 0.001, 0.002, 0.003, 0.005 and 0.01). Several values gave qualitatively similar group patterns in the latent space, and the value was chosen by inspection. Participants were split into five folds with `rsample::vfold_cv()` (v = 5, strata = dementia status). Each of five models was trained on four folds (1,992–1,994 participants, about 80%), and the held-out fold (497–499 participants, about 20%) served as validation data for early stopping and learning-rate reduction, to limit overfitting; there was no separate test set. Each trained encoder was then applied to all 2,491 participants, and the five latent means (z_mean) were averaged dimension by dimension to give one six-dimensional embedding per participant. Random seeds were fixed and TensorFlow's deterministic operations were enabled.]{.rev} The VAE was implemented using Keras 3 (keras3 v1.5.1) with the TensorFlow backend (v2.20.0) in R.

### Dementia Progression Score

Both UMAP and VAE produced 6-component embeddings, yielding 15 pairwise 2D projections. To quantify how well each 2D projection captured a smooth, directional trajectory through the six dementia categories, we developed a dementia progression score (DPS). DPS is the product of two components: path efficiency, which measures how straight the centroid path is, and mean directional cosine, which measures whether the path proceeds in the expected progression direction. The score ranges from $-1$ to $+1$, where values near $+1$ indicate centroids forming a straight-line path in the expected progression order, values near $0$ indicate no detectable progression signal, and values near $-1$ indicate reversed ordering.

For each dementia category in a given 2D projection, a density peak was identified using two-dimensional kernel density estimation (KDE) via `MASS::kde2d`. Grid points exceeding the 90th percentile of the estimated density surface were retained, and their mean coordinates served as the centroid for that category. The six centroids were then [placed in the clinical progression ordering, by baseline status and subsequent course]{.rev}: normal2mci, stable_normal, stable_mci, normal2incid, mci2incid, and prev_dementia[; normal2mci was placed before stable_normal because its EWAS effects ran opposite to those of the dementia groups (see Results)]{.rev}.

Given $n = 6$ ordered centroids $(x_i, y_i)$, step vectors and Euclidean distances between consecutive centroids were computed as:

$$\Delta x_i = x_{i+1} - x_i, \quad \Delta y_i = y_{i+1} - y_i, \quad d_i = \sqrt{\Delta x_i^2 + \Delta y_i^2}$$

The total path length and direct end-to-end distance, i.e., from the first transition normal2mci to the last prev_dementia, were defined as:

$$L_{\text{path}} = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} d_i, \qquad L_{\text{direct}} = \sqrt{(x_n - x_1)^2 + (y_n - y_1)^2}$$

Path efficiency, bounded in $[0, 1]$ by the triangle inequality, was computed as the ratio $E = L_{\text{direct}} / L_{\text{path}}$. A unit vector of progression direction was defined from the normal2mci centroid to the prev_dementia centroid:

$$\hat{\mathbf{p}} = \frac{1}{L_{\text{direct}}} \begin{pmatrix} x_n - x_1 \\ y_n - y_1 \end{pmatrix}$$

For each step, the cosine of the angle between the step vector and the progression direction was computed as:

$$\cos \theta_i = \frac{\Delta x_i \cdot \hat{p}_x + \Delta y_i \cdot \hat{p}_y}{d_i}$$

The mean directional cosine $C = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \cos \theta_i$ lies in $[-1, 1]$, where $+1$ indicates perfect forward alignment and $-1$ indicates complete reversal. The final score was computed as:

$$\text{DPS} = E \times C = \frac{L_{\text{direct}}}{L_{\text{path}}} \times \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} \cos \theta_i$$

To evaluate the statistical significance of the observed DPS in each 2D latent plane, we performed a label permutation test with 1,000 iterations. In each permutation, the dementia category labels were randomly shuffled across [participants]{.rev} while the embedding coordinates remained fixed, and DPS was recomputed for all 15 dimension pairs. This produced a null distribution under the hypothesis of no association between dementia group membership and methylation-derived embedding positions. Empirical [*P* values]{.rev} were computed as the proportion of permutations yielding a DPS greater than or equal to the observed value. DPS and the permutation test were applied identically to both UMAP and VAE embeddings, and dimension pairs were ranked by DPS. A path must be simultaneously efficient and correctly oriented to score near $+1$.

::: {.rev}
### Comparison with published blood EWAS

We compared AGES effect sizes with published blood EWAS of Alzheimer's disease (AD) that met three criteria: DNA methylation measured in whole blood on Illumina arrays, so that CpG sites could be matched to ours by probe identifier; contrasts of AD or MCI against cognitively normal (CN) controls, which parallel our contrasts against the stable normal group; and publicly available CpG-level effect estimates. We used two published resources, covering three cohorts, that met these criteria: the meta-analysis (META) of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Australian Imaging, Biomarkers, and Lifestyle (AIBL) cohorts [@RN44], whose genome-wide summary statistics we obtained from the MIAMI-AD database [@RN82], and the AddNeuroMed study [@RN24].

META combined 1,284 samples from 797 individuals (EPIC array) and reported, for 719,564 CpG sites, the odds ratio of AD per 0.01 increase in methylation β value, from logistic regression adjusted for age, sex, batch and cell-type proportions and combined by inverse-variance fixed-effects meta-analysis; we used the log~2~ odds ratio, and 717,520 of these sites were among our 799,149. AddNeuroMed (89 CN, 109 MCI and 86 AD participants; 450K array) published the 1,000 top-ranked CpG sites from an ANOVA of the three diagnostic groups; its effect estimate was the difference in mean β value between MCI or AD and controls after adjustment for age, sex, cell-type proportions and bisulfite-conversion batch, and 931 of its sites were among ours. We used the published summary statistics as released, without reprocessing; quality control and normalization are described in the original publications. In all three sets of effect estimates, a positive value indicates higher methylation in the case group.

CpG sites were selected on each comparator's own *P* value, so that the selection did not depend on the AGES results: META sites at six thresholds from *P* < 1.0 × 10^−4.5^ to *P* < 1.0 × 10^−2^ in steps of 0.5 on the −log~10~ scale, and all 931 matched AddNeuroMed sites, the only selection its published list allows. Each comparator contrast was compared with the AGES normal2incid, mci2incid and prevalent dementia contrasts. Because the studies report effects on different scales, only ranks and signs were tested: the Spearman correlation between the two sets of effect estimates, and a one-sided exact binomial test of whether more than half of the CpG sites had the same direction of effect. In each comparison, CpG sites outside the central 95% of either study's effect estimates (2.5% from each tail on each axis) were excluded before both tests.
:::

### Data analysis and statistical methods

Data analyses were primarily conducted using the tidyverse suite of packages in R version 4.5.2. [Spearman correlation tests (`stats::cor.test`), Welch t-tests (`stats::t.test`), one-way analyses of variance (`stats::anova` of a linear model) and one-sided binomial sign tests (`stats::binom.test`) used base R; the Kruskal–Wallis tests across *APOE* functional roles used rstatix (version 0.7.3), the chi-square test of *APOE* genotype by group used infer (version 1.1.0), and the group comparisons in @tbl-baseline used gtsummary (version 2.5.0; Kruskal–Wallis tests for continuous and chi-square tests for categorical variables). For 1,290 or fewer observations, `cor.test` by default computes Spearman *P* values with an Edgeworth series approximation (algorithm AS 89), which returns exactly 0 when the tail probability is very small; in those cases we report the *P* value from the asymptotic *t* approximation, which `cor.test` uses by default for larger samples, and we write *P* < 1.0 × 10^−300^ wherever that value is below the double-precision machine limit.]{.rev} Data visualization was implemented using ggplot2 (version 4.0.2) [@RN73] and its extensions (ggtext (version 0.1.2), ComplexUpset (version 1.3.3), geomtextpath (version 0.2.0)), with multi-panel figures assembled using the patchwork package (version 1.3.2). Tables were made using the `gt` package (version 1.3.0) [and, for @tbl-dementia-category and @tbl-baseline, flextable (version 0.10.0)]{.rev}.

### Reporting guidelines and data deposition

This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE guideline for observational
studies. Experimental design, sample annotation, array platform and the laboratory and
data-processing protocols are described above, following the MIAME recommendations for
array-based studies. Raw intensity data and the processed methylation matrix are not
deposited in a public repository: DNA methylation profiles are potentially identifiable,
and the AGES-Reykjavik consent terms and data-access policy do not permit open release.
Both are available to investigators under the controlled-access terms set out in the Data
availability statement, and summary statistics for the analyses reported here [are publicly
available (see Data availability)]{.rev}.
